activities.caption: bet before you read on — the flattening tax
activities.name: mapPeelPredict

config.q: You cannot flatten a curved surface without stretching, tearing or squashing it. Of shape, area, distance and direction, how many can one flat map preserve at once?
choices: All four, if the projection is drawn carefully
At most a few — most preserve one well and sacrifice the rest
None — every flat map is pure fiction
config.why: No flat map preserves all four; cartography's first rule is to choose the projection whose distortion hurts least for your purpose — maps are arguments, and a cartographer who understands the mechanics can see the argument.

activities.anchor: Because Mercator became the default classroom and web map
activities.caption: call the ratio — the Greenland lie
activities.name: mapAfricaEstimate

config.prompt: On Mercator, Greenland draws roughly the size of Africa. In reality Africa is about how many times larger?
config.why: About 14 times — 30.4 million km² against 2.2 million; the local stretch grows as 1 over the cosine of latitude, so at 60° everything draws twice as long and hence four times too big in area.
config.context: Generations internalised a world in which Europe and North America loom over the global south — a navigation tool that became a misleading default.

activities.anchor: The legitimate criticism is that a navigation tool became a general-purpose world map
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the projection hearing
activities.name: mapMercatorSpot

config.prompt: One line of this projection hearing is wrong — click it:
lines: Mercator (1569) preserves angles: any straight line on it is a constant compass bearing.
The area inflation grows toward the poles, in proportion to 1 over the cosine of latitude.
Mercator was designed in 1569 to flatter Europe and diminish the global south.
Equal-area projections (Gall-Peters, Mollweide, Albers) solve size at the cost of sheared shapes.
Compromise projections such as Robinson and the Winkel tripel minimise total distortion without eliminating any.
config.correction: Mercator built it for compass navigation, three centuries before the countries it allegedly flatters existed in their modern form — the inflation is a mathematical consequence of preserving bearings, not a political choice.
config.why: The fix is choosing the right projection for the purpose, not discarding the wrong-shamed one — and for showing the poles, azimuthal projections centred on a point beat everything.

activities.anchor: Scale expresses how much reality one map unit represents
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the scale word-trap
activities.name: mapScaleCloze

config.text: On a 1:50,000 map, 1 cm equals %%0%% m; 'large scale' (1:10,000) shows %%1%% areas in great detail; 'small scale' (1:1,000,000) shows large areas in little detail — the fraction is literally bigger or smaller.
config.hint: The misconception says 'large scale' means a map of a large region — it is exactly backwards.

activities.anchor: From contours you can compute real quantities
activities.caption: pair each contour pattern with the ground it hides
activities.name: mapContourMatch

config.prompt: Reading the land from contour lines — pair pattern with meaning:

pairs.left: a V of contours pointing uphill
pairs.right: a valley — rivers cut the V

config.why: Closed rings without hachures mark hills — and a cross-section turns the contour data into a picture of what a walker or road engineer will actually face.

activities.anchor: Choosing is a real design decision
activities.caption: file each layer: vector or raster
activities.name: mapVectorBuckets

config.prompt: Which storage fits each dataset? File them:

items.label: wells and crimes recorded as points
roads and rivers recorded as lines
parcels and lakes recorded as polygons
a road network queried for junction connections
a landslide susceptibility model (slope, soil and rain per cell)

config.why: Boundary and network data is almost always vector; continuous environmental surfaces are almost always raster — and each conversion between the two trades precision for convenience.

activities.anchor: for a pipeline or a landing strip is an expensive category of error
activities.caption: call the drift — the datum trap
activities.name: mapDatumEstimate

config.prompt: North American data stored in the old NAD27 datum, read in a modern system, can land how far from the truth?
config.why: 100 m or more — the datum is the mathematical model of Earth's shape that coordinates are measured against, and mixing them is an expensive category of error.
config.context: GPS satellites give any phone metre-level position from a constellation of over thirty satellites; the modern skill is knowing which coordinate system your data was born in.

activities.caption: pin the stretch — longitude's shrinking degree
activities.name: mapLongitudePlace

config.prompt: A degree of latitude runs about 111 km anywhere. At 60°N, how much ground does one degree of longitude cover?
config.why: About 55 km — longitude shrinks with the cosine of the latitude, reaching zero at the poles, which is why serious spatial work is done in metre-based projected systems like UTM.
